opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue in robot learning right now is data. If you look at what's driven progress in language and vision, it's scale — internet-scale text and images. Robotics doesn't have that. There's no internet of robot actions sitting around for us to scrape. So the question becomes: where do we get the data?

The default answer for the past few years has been teleoperation: you have a person puppeteer a robot and record the trajectories. That works, and it's given us some impressive results, but it's fundamentally bottlenecked. You need the physical robot, you need a trained operator, every hour of data costs a lot of money and effort, and the data is tied to that specific embodiment. If you change the robot, a lot of that investment doesn't transfer cleanly. It's very hard to see how that scales to billions of interactions.

Simulation is another option, and it's useful, but the sim-to-real gap for contact-rich manipulation — deformable objects, friction, cluttered scenes — is still really hard to close, and building diverse simulated environments is its own bottleneck.

Humans, on the other hand, are already doing manipulation everywhere, all the time. Eight billion people cooking, folding laundry, assembling things, using tools. That's an enormous, naturally occurring source of exactly the behavior we want robots to learn. And with things like wearable cameras and smart glasses becoming more common, we can actually capture that data passively, in the wild, at a scale teleoperation could never match. You don't need a robot in the loop at all.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that human data captures more than motion. It captures intent, task structure, how people recover from mistakes, how they adapt to new objects and environments. That diversity is precisely what robots lack today — they're brittle when they leave the lab.

Of course, there's a real challenge: the embodiment gap. Human hands aren't robot grippers, human bodies move differently, and the camera viewpoints differ. So a lot of our research is about how to bridge that — learning representations and policies that treat human and robot data as different embodiments of a shared underlying behavior, co-training on both, aligning the action spaces, so that a small amount of robot data plus a large amount of human data gets you much further than robot data alone. And what we've been seeing is that this works — the human data meaningfully improves generalization to new scenes and objects.

So to me it's a scaling argument at heart. If you believe that general-purpose manipulation requires data at scale, then you have to find a source that scales, and human data is the only one I see that's both abundant and directly relevant to the physical tasks we care about.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that manipulation needs data at scale, says teleoperation cannot match human data’s scale, and identifies human data as the only source it sees as both abundant and directly relevant.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, the honest answer starts with what hasn't worked, or at least what hasn't scaled. If you look at where the big breakthroughs in AI came from, language and vision, they came from enormous amounts of data that already existed in the world. Nobody had to sit down and generate the internet for the purpose of training a language model. Robotics never had that. Every robot dataset we have is something someone painstakingly collected, usually through teleoperation, usually one robot, one lab, a few hundred or a few thousand demonstrations. That's orders of magnitude short of what we'd need.

And the alternatives all have real limits. Simulation is great for things like locomotion, where contact is relatively simple and the physics is forgiving. But for manipulation, the moment you have deformable objects, liquids, cluttered scenes, tool use, the sim-to-real gap gets really painful, and building those simulated environments is itself a huge labor cost. Pure reinforcement learning in the real world is slow and sometimes dangerous, and you still have to design the reward. Teleoperation gives you beautiful, in-distribution data, but it's bottlenecked on the number of robots and operators you can afford.

Human data breaks that bottleneck. There are billions of people doing manipulation tasks every single day, with dexterity that no robot comes close to, and a lot of it is already captured in video. Cooking, assembling furniture, folding laundry, repairing things. The diversity of objects, scenes, and strategies is exactly the long tail that robots fail on. So the argument is really about scale and coverage. If we believe the lesson from the rest of AI, that generality comes from broad data, then human activity is the only source of manipulation data that is actually broad.

Now, I want to be careful, because the obvious objection is the embodiment gap. A human hand is not a robot gripper, a human arm doesn't have the same kinematics, and in a video you don't get the forces, the torques, the low-level actions. That's a real problem, and I'd say most of the interesting research right now is about what you extract from human data rather than trying to copy it directly. You can learn affordances, where to grasp, how objects respond. You can learn task structure, the sequence of subgoals that makes up a long task. You can learn visual representations that transfer across embodiments. And then you bridge the last mile with a much smaller amount of robot data, or with retargeting, or with wearable devices that get human demonstrations closer to robot observations.

So I wouldn't frame it as human data instead of everything else. It's human data as the foundation, because it's the only thing that scales, with simulation and robot data filling in the pieces it can't give you. The bet is that robotics will follow the same arc as language and vision: find the data that already exists at scale, figure out how to learn from it, and then specialize. And human behavior is that data.

r001.rationale: The response says human activity is “the only source of manipulation data that is actually broad” and “the only thing that scales,” while describing simulation and robot data as supplements.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest reason is scale. Humans manipulate objects all day long—cooking, cleaning, assembling things—and those activities contain a tremendous amount of information about how the physical world works. If we can learn from that experience, we don’t have to collect every example by having someone operate a robot.

And it’s not just the amount of data. Human behavior gives us examples of what’s useful to do: how to break a task into steps, which objects matter, and how to recover when something goes wrong. Those are things we want robots to learn alongside the physical skills.

The challenge is that watching a human do something doesn’t directly tell a robot how to do it. Our bodies are different, and video doesn’t necessarily reveal the forces or contact details involved. So I see human data as a rich foundation, with robot experience providing the grounding. The exciting possibility is that a robot could learn broadly from people, then need much less robot-specific data to turn that knowledge into action.

r001.rationale: The response says human data can reduce the need for robot-specific examples, but it also describes robot experience as providing grounding. It does not claim human data is the only source that can scale sufficiently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest reason is scale. Humans are already doing the kinds of manipulation tasks we want robots to do, every day, in an incredible variety of environments. We handle different objects, recover from mistakes, and adapt when things don’t go exactly as expected. There’s a lot of useful information in that experience.

With robot data, you have to put a robot in an environment and collect demonstrations or let it practice. That’s valuable, but it’s expensive and difficult to scale. Human data gives us a much broader source of examples of what successful interaction with the world looks like.

The challenge is that a human hand and a robot gripper are different. You can’t simply copy the motion. But you can potentially learn things like what matters in a task, how actions should be sequenced, and what changes you need to produce in the environment. Then robot experience can help ground that knowledge in the robot’s own body. That combination is what makes human data so promising to me.

r001.rationale: The response says human data offers a broader source of examples and is easier to scale than robot data, but does not claim it is the only source that can scale sufficiently.
